design_detail: Prospective, web-based observational study with opportunity sampling. Adults who planned to take a psychedelic on their own initiative signed up at a study website and completed five online surveys: about 1 week before (traits, intentions, well-being), within 1 day before (state of mind, the 'set' items), about 1 day after (drug taken, self-estimated dose, setting, and the acute experience) and 2 and 4 weeks after the planned date (well-being). Set, setting and intention items written by the authors were reduced to principal components. Predictors of the acute experience were modelled together in a multivariate linear regression of standardized variables; well-being over time in linear mixed models. No control group; the drug, amount, purity, setting and company were the participants' own choices.
can_establish: Whether, among people who had already decided to take a psychedelic and who completed the surveys, a state of mind rated the day before, and intentions and traits rated a week before, were associated with how mystical, challenging or visually intense they rated the experience about a day later, with the predictors and the self-estimated dose adjusted for one another.
cannot_establish: That preparation, mood or intentions cause a better or less difficult experience (observational, with the dose estimated after the experience and drug type, psychiatric history and other drugs taken not in the model); that the experience caused the rise in well-being (no control group, 68% lost by four weeks, baseline well-being below population norms, so regression to the mean is possible); or anything about the people who dropped out, who were not compared with completers.

sample.recruitment: Opportunity sample: online advertisements on Facebook, Twitter, email newsletters and online drug forums (two Reddit forums on LSD and on psychedelics) linking to the study website; participants gave the expected date of their experience and were sent timed survey links by email (Materials and methods › Participant recruitment and dissemination of the study, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: aged 18 or over, good comprehension of English, an intention to take in the near future a drug the authors list as a classic psychedelic (psilocybin mushrooms or truffles, LSD or 1P-LSD, ayahuasca, DMT or 5-MeO-DMT, salvia divinorum, mescaline, iboga or ibogaine). No exclusion criteria are stated; psychiatric history was asked about but did not exclude.
sample.demographics: Baseline (n = 654): 485 men (74.2%), 165 women (25.2%), 4 other; age 28.9 (SD 10.4); 39.1% students; 49.7% with a bachelor's or postgraduate degree (editors' sum); 30.4% from the United States, 19.6% the United Kingdom, 9.2% Denmark; 214 (32.7%) reported having ever been diagnosed with a psychiatric illness; 62 (9.5%) had never used a psychedelic and 404 (61.8%) had used one 6 or more times (editors' sum). Day-after survey (n = 379): LSD or 1P-LSD 183 (48.3%), psilocybin 109 (28.8%), ayahuasca 42 (11.1%), DMT or 5-MeO-DMT 12 (3.2%), mescaline 10 (2.6%), other 23 (6.1%) (Tables 1 and 2).
sample.attrition: 654 at baseline, 535 one day before (81.8%), 379 about one day after (58.0%), 315 at two weeks (48.2%) and 212 at four weeks (32.4%) (editors' percentages). Reasons for dropping out were not collected and completers were not compared with dropouts; the authors say they intend to do so. The acute-experience regression appears to rest on about 198 people (editors' inference from the error degrees of freedom). Of the day-before items, the first ten were answered by 535 people, 'strong expectations' by 386 and 'clear intention' by 326 (Table 3, footnote).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected people planning a psychedelic experience, reached through social media and drug forums; the authors report the sample was positively biased towards psychedelic use and more so towards therapeutic use (Figure 2, an image not viewed), and that completing every survey may have favoured well-prepared, motivated people (Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph). 90.5% had used psychedelics before. With 42% lost before the experience was reported and no comparison of completers and dropouts, the associations describe completers only; if people who had difficult experiences were less likely to report them, the challenging-experience findings would be biased in an unknown direction.

exposure.measurement: About a week before (survey 1): absorption (Modified Tellegen Absorption Scale, 25 scored items); openness and emotional stability (Ten-Item Personality Inventory, two items per trait); trait anxiety (six-item short form of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory); suggestibility (Short Suggestibility Scale, 21 items); stubbornness (Stubborn Opinionatedness scale, 16 items); number of lifetime psychedelic uses; a self-rating of being highly experienced with psychedelics; and ten motives rated from 'not at all' to 'very much', reduced to three components: 'spiritual connection' (spiritual, religious, nature, therapeutic), 'recreation' (fun or party, social, curiosity) and 'emotional' (to escape or to confront difficult emotions; medicinal). Within a day before (survey 2): 12 visual-analogue items written for the study, reduced to 'set' (feeling comfortable, open, well prepared, not anxious, in a good mood, ready to surrender, not preoccupied with duties), 'setting' (a good feeling about the people who will be present and about the environment) and 'clear intentions' (strong expectations and a clear intention). About a day after (survey 3): the drug taken, a self-estimated dose, and whether the setting was a retreat or designed with a therapeutic aim, combined into one yes-or-no 'therapeutic environment' variable (Materials and methods › The surveys; Tables 3 and 4; Discussion › Set, setting, and drug dose…, 4th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not controlled. Dose was estimated by the participant after the experience, in five response categories the survey anchored to LSD equivalents (low, up to 50 µg; moderate, up to 100; high, up to 200; very high, up to 300; extremely high, over 300); at the day-after survey 39 (10.3%) chose low, 144 (38.0%) moderate, 135 (35.6%) high, 37 (9.8%) very high and 24 (6.3%) extremely high (Table 2). Route was not recorded. At the two- and four-week surveys, 88 and a further 29 participants reported more than one psychedelic experience during the study (Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported: the paper does not say whether alcohol, cannabis or other drugs were taken with the psychedelic. Having more than one psychedelic experience during the study was among the candidate covariates for the well-being models, which kept only significant covariates; it is not in the final models.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (naturalistic use). How recently participants had last used a psychedelic before baseline is not reported.

comparison.controls: None. Predictors are compared across participants within the cohort; well-being is compared within participants over time and with published population norms for the Warwick-Edinburgh scale (mean 50.7, 95% CI 50.3 to 51.1).
comparison.matching: Not applicable. In the acute-experience regression all 16 predictors were entered together (lifetime uses, self-rated experience, five traits, three intention components, set, setting, clear intentions, self-estimated dose, therapeutic environment). Covariates for the well-being models were chosen by statistical significance from age, sex, employment, education, lifetime uses, further psychedelic experiences during the study and four attitude items.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not in the acute-experience model: drug type (LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca and others differ in duration and character), psychiatric history (32.7% reported a diagnosis), age and sex. Not measured: the actual amount and purity, other drugs taken, who was actually present and what they did, and preparation practices.

outcomes.instruments: Acute experience, self-rated online in survey 3, sent one day after the planned experience (the Introduction says within a few days after): the Mystical Experience Questionnaire (MEQ30, total score), the Challenging Experience Questionnaire (CEQ, total score), and a 'visual effects' score the authors built from three subscales (elementary imagery, complex imagery, audio-visual synaesthesia) of the Altered States of Consciousness rating scale (OAV or 11D-ASC). Well-being: Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale (WEMWBS, 14 items) at baseline and at two and four weeks (Materials and methods › Survey 3 › Measures; Survey 1 › Measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: Validated questionnaires for the acute experience and well-being; a population norm for the WEMWBS (England and Scotland) is used for comparison. The set, setting, clear-intention and motive items were written for this study; their only structural check is the principal component analysis (set and setting: KMO 0.800, three components explaining 54.33% of variance; intentions: KMO 0.695, 55.14%). The visual-effects composite is specific to this study. Openness and emotional stability rest on two items each.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Challenging experience' is the CEQ total and 'mystical-type experience' the MEQ total, both continuous, rated by the participant about a day after; no threshold for a 'bad trip' or a 'complete' mystical experience is used. The predictors set, setting and clear intentions are component scores from items rated within a day before taking the drug; intentions and traits were rated about a week before. Dose and therapeutic environment were reported after the experience.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; alpha 0.05 for every test. Four outcomes (MEQ, CEQ, visual effects, WEMWBS), with 48 predictor coefficients in Table 7 (16 predictors by 3 outcomes), 15 in Table 5 and 57 in Table 6 (19 predictors by 3 time points), and t-tests on 18 variables comparing people whose well-being fell with the rest (editors' counts).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: all measures were self-reported online by participants who knew what they had taken and in what circumstances. Completion at the intended times could not be verified, and the day-before survey could be filled in on paper and transferred later (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Acute experience (Table 7; standardized coefficients with all predictors adjusted for one another; R2 0.342 for MEQ, 0.324 for CEQ, 0.211 for visual effects). Challenging experience: set beta = -0.324 (SE 0.070, p < 0.001); recreation intentions -0.224 (SE 0.081, p = 0.006); setting -0.137 (SE 0.075, p = 0.070); clear intentions -0.134 (p = 0.088); absorption 0.215 (SE 0.082, p = 0.010); self-estimated dose 0.219 (SE 0.077, p = 0.005); trait anxiety 0.140 (p = 0.211); therapeutic environment 0.021 (p = 0.813). Mystical-type experience: absorption 0.347 (SE 0.076, p < 0.001); dose 0.285 (SE 0.071, p < 0.001); clear intentions 0.180 (SE 0.072, p = 0.013); spiritual connection 0.153 (p = 0.054); set 0.014 (p = 0.835); lifetime uses -0.144 (p = 0.086). Visual effects: dose 0.327 (p < 0.001); absorption 0.227 (p = 0.003); clear intentions 0.155 (p = 0.033). Openness, emotional stability, trait anxiety, suggestibility, stubbornness, lifetime uses, self-rated experience and therapeutic environment were associated with none of the three. Well-being (WEMWBS): 49.0 (95% CI 48.3 to 49.7) at baseline, 52.6 (51.8 to 53.4) at two weeks, 51.8 (50.6 to 53.0) at four weeks; quadratic trend F(154) = 23.20, p < 0.001 (editors' calculation: +3.6 and +2.8 points, in shrinking samples). MEQ by time interaction F(232) = 3.03, reported p < 0.050; MEQ coefficient on WEMWBS 0.948 at baseline (p = 0.083), 2.287 at two weeks (p < 0.001) and 1.608 at four weeks (p = 0.015). CEQ was negatively associated with WEMWBS at every time point, baseline included (B = -1.435, -1.975, -1.252), with no interaction with time. In the full model (Table 6) only trait anxiety and lifetime uses interacted with time, and the MEQ coefficients were -0.258, -0.102 and 0.002.
analysis.covariates: Acute-experience model: the 16 predictors adjusted for one another. Well-being models: lifetime uses and the self-rated experience item, retained because they were significant among the candidate covariates listed under comparison.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned. Hypotheses are stated in the Introduction (well-being higher at two weeks than at baseline; mystical-type experience predicting the change); the analyses of predictors of the acute experience are exploratory. Many more measures were collected and are to be reported elsewhere (Materials and methods › The surveys, 1st paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only 'key measures of interest' are reported, with the rest deferred to future papers; covariates were selected by significance; the visual-effects composite and the set, setting and intention components were built in this sample. The correlation matrix is in a supplement (a Word file) that was not read.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The acute-experience regression has 16 predictors on about 198 complete cases.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among people who completed the surveys, feeling comfortable, open, prepared, unanxious and in a good mood within the day before (the 'set' component) was associated with lower challenging-experience scores about a day after (beta -0.32), as were recreational or social intentions (beta -0.22); clear intentions and expectations were associated with higher mystical-type and visual scores (beta 0.18 and 0.16); trait absorption and self-estimated dose were associated with higher scores on all three measures, mystical and challenging alike. Set was not associated with mystical-type experience, and a retreat or therapeutic setting with none of the acute measures. Mean well-being rose from 49.0 to 52.6 at two weeks while the sample fell from 654 to 315, with no comparison group; mystical-type ratings were associated with that rise in the smaller model (interaction p about 0.050), not once traits, intentions, set and setting were added.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says absorption and higher doses 'promoted' all aspects of the experience and that a positive set and recreational intentions decrease the likelihood of a challenging experience; the Discussion says the principle that psychedelics enhance well-being even in healthy people “appears to be supported by the present study's data”, and the Strengths section that the prospective design makes causal inference easier; the Conclusions say baseline traits explained the greatest proportion of the variance in well-being change. Gaps: (1) causal verbs for observational associations, with the dose estimated after the experience and drug type, psychiatric history and other drugs not adjusted; (2) without a control group, and with heavy attrition and a baseline below the population norm (those whose well-being rose had lower baseline scores, the pattern regression to the mean produces), the well-being rise cannot be attributed to the drug; (3) no partition of variance by type of predictor is reported, so the 'greatest proportion' statement has no supporting statistic; (4) the mystical-type effect on well-being highlighted in the abstract did not survive the fuller model, which the Discussion acknowledges; (5) the primary interaction is at p = 0.050, not below it. The Implications section turns these associations into practical recommendations for therapeutic use.

timeline.event: Leary et al.: apprehension before psilocybin correlated negatively with the pleasantness of the experience (described in this paper's Introduction).

Studerus et al. pooled 23 psilocybin laboratory studies: absorption and feeling well beforehand predicted peak experiences; younger age, emotional excitability beforehand and a PET scanner predicted challenging experiences (as described in this paper's Introduction).
Aday et al. systematic review: this study is its only prospective naturalistic source of set and intention predictors (its Table 1 misprints two of this study's signs).
Studerus et al., MDMA pooled laboratory analysis: anxious-depressed mood measured just before dosing predicted higher acute anxiety scores.
Vizeli et al., LSD pooled laboratory analysis: anxiety rated just before dosing predicted acute anxiety; the authors call this consistent with the present study.

replication.where_it_stands: Still the main prospective study of set, intentions and setting in self-directed psychedelic use found for this page. Its central acute finding, a better state of mind the day before going with fewer challenging experiences, agrees in direction with laboratory analyses that measured mood before dosing (Studerus 2012 for psilocybin, as described here; Studerus 2021 for MDMA; Vizeli 2024 for LSD), which is why the status is partial: those are conceptual replications in controlled settings with other instruments. No study has repeated the naturalistic prospective design with the same measures, and the well-being findings have no comparison group. The authors describe the design as never before used in psychedelic research (Discussion › Strengths, 1st paragraph, as of 2018); where the claims call it the only prospective study, they mean among the sources read for this page, not in the literature as a whole.

funding.funder: The paper states that the authors received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication of the article; RC-H (R.L. Carhart-Harris) is supported by the Alex Mosley Charitable Trust.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that the research was conducted without commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest. The reviewer FB declared to the handling editor a past co-authorship with several of the authors (MK, LR, DN, RL, RC-H).
funding.affiliations_note: Psychedelic Research Group and the Computational, Cognitive and Clinical Neuroimaging Laboratory, Imperial College London; S. Russ at Dickinson State University, whose work inspired the set items. Handling editor N. Andrews; reviewers F.S. Barrett and E. Nalivaiko. The study website recruits for further online studies by the same group.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered prospective cohort, recruited from the same sources, that measures set and intentions with validated instruments before use, records the substance (confirmed by drug checking where possible), amount, other drugs and setting at the time rather than afterwards, follows dropouts as well as completers, and includes a comparison group who do not take a psychedelic; and randomized trials of preparation, for example a structured preparation session against none, in clinical or laboratory settings with challenging-experience scores as a prespecified outcome.

domains.note: Predictors were adjusted for one another and for self-estimated dose, but not for drug type, psychiatric history, age or sex, and other drugs taken were not measured; drug type in particular plausibly affects both preparation and challenging-experience scores. Covariates for the well-being models were selected by significance.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Set and intentions were measured before use, a strength, but with unvalidated items; openness and emotional stability with two items each; completion times unverifiable. For dose the risk is high: it was estimated after the experience, when intensity may colour the estimate (the authors say so).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study (or into the analysis)
domains.note: Self-selected, experienced, positively disposed sample from social media and drug forums; entry did not depend on the outcome, but the sample is atypical.

What sitters or companions did during the experience, and any redosing or other drugs, were not recorded; for well-being, 88 and a further 29 participants had additional psychedelic experiences during follow-up.

58% reported the experience and about 30% of the baseline sample entered the acute-experience regression; 32% remained at four weeks; no analysis of dropouts. Mixed models assume data missing at random, which is doubtful if difficult experiences affected continuation.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Validated questionnaires, but self-rated about a day later by people who knew their own preparation and intentions; the same person rated set and outcome, so a shared optimistic or anxious style could inflate associations.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Unregistered and exploratory for the acute predictors; many measures collected and only some reported; components and a composite built in the sample; no correction for multiple tests.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High because of unadjusted confounding (drug type, psychiatric history, unmeasured other drugs) and heavy, unanalysed attrition, with further concerns about a retrospectively estimated dose and shared self-report of predictors and outcomes. The prospective timing of the set and intention measures is a real strength over retrospective surveys. The source can be cited for the association, among people completing the surveys, between a better state of mind the day before (and recreational or social intentions) and lower challenging-experience scores, and between clear intentions and higher mystical-type scores, always as associations; and for the finding that absorption and self-estimated dose went with more intense experiences of every kind. It should not be cited for causal effects of preparation, for an effect of a therapeutic or retreat setting (the null finding rests on a loosely defined yes-or-no item), or for psychedelics raising well-being.

key_findings.finding: Design facts: five online surveys, about 1 week before, within 1 day before, about 1 day after, and 2 and 4 weeks after a self-chosen psychedelic experience; completed by 654, 535, 379, 315 and 212 people. Setting questions (retreat, therapeutic design, party-type setting, number of people present, someone looking after the participant) were asked in survey 3, but their distribution is shown only in Figure 3 (an image not viewable in this reading; values not extracted).
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Study design, 1st paragraph; Survey 3 › Measures, 1st paragraph; Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph; Figure 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Baseline sample (survey 1, n = 654; Table 1): 485 men (74.2%), mean age 28.9 (SD 10.4); 214 (32.7% of 654; 36.0% of the 595 who answered) reported a past psychiatric diagnosis; 62 (9.5%) had never used a psychedelic and 189 (28.9%) had used one more than 21 times. Drug at the day-after survey (n = 379; Table 2): LSD or 1P-LSD 183 (48.3%), psilocybin 109 (28.8%), ayahuasca 42 (11.1%), DMT or 5-MeO-DMT 12 (3.2%), mescaline 10 (2.6%), other 23 (6.1%).

The 'set' component (31.12% of item variance) loaded on feeling comfortable (0.765), open (0.708) and well prepared (0.648), on feeling anxious (-0.635), being in a good mood (0.619), being ready to surrender (0.583) and being preoccupied with work or duties (-0.392); 'setting' (12.49%) on a good feeling about the group and the main person looking after the participant and about the environment; 'clear intentions' (10.72%) on strong expectations and a clear intention. All rated 0-100 within a day before use.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 and footnote; Results › Principle component analysis: set and setting, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Challenging experience (CEQ total, self-rated about a day after) was lower with a better set the day before (beta = -0.324, SE 0.070, p < 0.001) and with recreational or social intentions rated a week before (beta = -0.224, SE 0.081, p = 0.006); the setting component showed a non-significant trend (beta = -0.137, p = 0.070). Higher with absorption (beta = 0.215, p = 0.010) and self-estimated dose (beta = 0.219, p = 0.005). Model R2 0.324.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predicting challenging experiences, 1st paragraph; Results › Predicting acute psychedelic experience measures, 1st paragraph; Table 7 (challenging experience panel); Results › Predicting visual effects, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mystical-type experience (MEQ30 total) was higher with absorption (beta = 0.347, p < 0.001), self-estimated dose (beta = 0.285, p < 0.001) and clear intentions (beta = 0.180, p = 0.013), with a trend for spiritual-connection intentions (beta = 0.153, p = 0.054); set was unrelated (beta = 0.014, p = 0.835). Visual effects were higher with dose (0.327), absorption (0.227) and clear intentions (0.155, p = 0.033). R2 0.342 and 0.211.
key_findings.locator: Results › Predicting mystical-type experiences, 1st paragraph; Results › Predicting visual effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 7 (mystical-type and visual panels)

key_findings.finding: No statistically significant association (p < 0.05) with any acute measure in the model of about 198 people: openness, emotional stability, trait anxiety, suggestibility, stubbornness, number of lifetime uses (closest: mystical-type experience −0.144, p = 0.086), self-rated experience, and being in a retreat or therapeutically designed setting (challenging experience beta = 0.021, p = 0.813), a variable the authors formed by grouping two yes-or-no questions asked after the experience (a psychedelic retreat; a setting designed with a therapeutic objective). The authors caution that retreats were grouped with therapeutic settings and that the term was not defined for participants.
key_findings.locator: Table 7; Materials and methods › Survey 3 › Measures, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Set, setting, and drug dose as predictors for acute psychedelic experience measures, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion › Trait-variables as predictors for the acute psychedelic experience measures, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Well-being (WEMWBS) averaged 49.0 (95% CI 48.3 to 49.7) at baseline, below the population norm of 50.7 (50.3 to 51.1), then 52.6 (51.8 to 53.4) at two weeks and 51.8 (50.6 to 53.0) at four weeks; quadratic trend F(154) = 23.20, p < 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in well-being scores, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Means at each time point come from shrinking samples (654, 315, 212) with no control group.

key_findings.finding: Well-being fell at two weeks in 85 people and was unchanged or higher in 194 (editors' calculation: 30.5% fell); the groups did not differ in mystical-type or challenging-experience scores, only in baseline well-being, which was lower in those whose well-being rose (reported as F(277) = 6.95, p < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Splitting participants based on change in well-being, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: For 1 and 277 degrees of freedom F = 6.95 gives p = 0.009 (editors' calculation); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: In the model with acute measures only, mystical-type experience interacted with time on well-being (F(232) = 3.03, reported p < 0.050): coefficients 0.948 at baseline (p = 0.083), 2.287 at two weeks (p < 0.001), 1.608 at four weeks (p = 0.015). Challenging experience went with lower well-being at every time point, baseline included (B = -1.435, -1.975, -1.252), without interacting with time. More lifetime uses went with lower well-being at two weeks (B = -1.378, p = 0.010).
key_findings.locator: Results › Acute psychedelic experience measures predicting well-being changes, 1st paragraph; Table 5

key_findings.finding: In the full model, only trait anxiety (interaction F(172) = 3.93) and lifetime uses (F(106) = 6.11) interacted with time; mystical-type experience no longer predicted well-being (B = -0.258, -0.102, 0.002). Feeling good about the setting and people the day before went with higher well-being at two weeks (B = 1.206, p = 0.037) and spiritual-connection intentions with higher well-being at every time point (B = 1.428, 1.365, 1.872).
key_findings.locator: Results › Traits, set and setting, intentions and acute psychedelic experience measures predicting well-being changes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 6

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: survey timing could not be confirmed; the sample may favour well-prepared, motivated people; attrition reasons were not collected; dose was reported after the experience and may reflect its intensity; well-being is a loosely defined construct.

Lifetime number of psychedelic uses correlated negatively with the change in well-being from baseline to two weeks (printed as r(279) = −0.23, p < 0.001): people with more earlier experience improved less; the authors link this to their higher baseline well-being (printed as r(654) = 0.21 with lifetime uses).
key_findings.note: Bivariate. The bracketed numbers are sample sizes rather than degrees of freedom (see the reporting issue on r(653)). Consistent with the lifetime-uses by time interaction in the full model (Table 6: two weeks −2.215, SE 0.673, p = 0.001).

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison of people whose well-being fell with the rest is described as an independent t-test but reported as F(277) = 6.95, p < 0.001; for 1 and 277 degrees of freedom (t = 2.64) the p value is 0.009 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Splitting participants based on change in well-being, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The baseline difference is real but weaker than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The primary test that mystical-type experience predicts the change in well-being is reported as F(232) = 3.03, p < 0.050; with a three-level time factor (2 and 232 degrees of freedom) p = 0.050 (editors' calculation), at rather than below the threshold.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Acute psychedelic experience measures predicting well-being changes, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline link between mystical-type experience and well-being change is borderline even before the full model removes it.

reporting_issues.issue: F statistics are printed with a single degrees-of-freedom value (for example F(181), F(154), F(172), F(106)); for Table 7 the F values equal the squared t values, so they are 1-df tests, and the error df of 181 with 16 predictors implies about 198 complete cases.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Predicting acute psychedelic experience measures to Predicting visual effects; Table 7
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysed sample for the acute-experience findings is about 198, not the 379 who reported the experience; the paper does not say so.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists 214 (32.7%) ever diagnosed with a psychiatric illness and 381 (67.3%) never diagnosed; 381 is 58.3% of 654, the rows sum to 595, and 67.3% is simply 100 minus 32.7 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: 59 people with no answer are unaccounted for; the share with a diagnosis is 32.7% of all or 36.0% of those answering.

reporting_issues.issue: The intention to confront difficult emotions is reported to correlate with the CEQ at r(653) = 0.22, but the CEQ was collected only at survey 3 (379 respondents), so neither the n nor the df can be 653; elsewhere r(654) is printed for a correlation on 654 people, whose df would be 652.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion › Acute psychedelic experience measures as predictors for change in well-being, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample behind that correlation is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say lifetime uses were not related to baseline well-being (B = 0.392, p = 0.479 in Table 6; -0.030, p = 0.958 in Table 5), while the Discussion says more lifetime use went with higher baseline well-being (r = 0.21, p < 0.001); the models also contain the closely related self-rated-experience item.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Traits, set and setting…, 1st paragraph; Tables 5 and 6; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The bivariate and adjusted associations disagree without comment, so neither should be cited alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say all variables were standardized, but the well-being models have intercepts near 50 (Tables 5 and 6), so their outcome is in raw WEMWBS points and their coefficients are points per standard deviation of the predictor (editors' reading); only Table 7 is fully standardized.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Materials and methods › Statistical analyses, 7th paragraph; Tables 5 to 7
reporting_issues.consequence: The coefficients in Tables 5 and 6 and in Table 7 are on different scales.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions say baseline traits explained the greatest proportion of the variance in well-being change, but no variance explained by type of predictor is reported for the well-being models; Table 6 gives coefficients only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement has no supporting statistic in the paper.

disagreements.first_pass: Sample: 74.2% men, mean age 28.9 (SD 10.4); 32.7% reported a past psychiatric diagnosis; 9.5% had never used a psychedelic and 28.9% had used one more than 21 times. Drug at the day-after survey (n = 379): LSD or 1P-LSD 48.3%, psilocybin 28.8%, ayahuasca 11.1%, DMT or 5-MeO-DMT 3.2%, mescaline 2.6%, other 6.1%.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 269, targeted check of the claim anchor built from this finding (cl_xc_mindset_before, anchor 1): the men and diagnosis shares are of the 654 at baseline, not the 379; Table 1's diagnosis rows sum to 595 (36.0% of those answering).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed against Table 1 (demographic data collected at the first time point, total 654) and Table 2 (total 379) in the saved PMC copy. The finding now names each denominator and gives the counts, so the two samples cannot be mixed again; no number changed.

disagreements.first_pass: Not associated with any acute measure: openness, emotional stability, trait anxiety, suggestibility, stubbornness, number of lifetime uses, self-rated experience, and being in a retreat or therapeutically designed setting (challenging experience beta = 0.021, p = 0.813). The authors caution that retreats were grouped with therapeutic settings and that the term was not defined for participants.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 269 (confirmed, wording): 'not associated' means no coefficient with p below 0.05 in a model of about 198 people (lifetime uses with mystical-type score −0.144, p = 0.086); 'no statistically significant association' would be more exact. For cl_xc_setting_support the same reader noted that the retreat or therapeutic-setting variable came from two separate yes-or-no questions grouped into one variable.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after checking Table 7, Survey 3 › Measures (1st paragraph: separate yes-or-no items on a retreat and on a therapeutic design) and Discussion › Set, setting, and drug dose…, 4th paragraph (people in a retreat grouped with those reporting a therapeutic setting) in the saved PMC copy. Wording changed, the item structure added, and the Survey 3 locator added.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 269, missed: Discussion, 2nd paragraph: lifetime number of psychedelic uses correlated negatively with the change in well-being, r(279) = −0.23, p < 0.001 (people with more experience improved less), consistent with the lifetime-uses by time interaction in Table 6; relevant wherever the well-being rise is cited.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted: found as stated in the saved PMC copy (Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table 6, lifetime uses × two weeks −2.215, p = 0.001). Added as a key finding with a note on the bracketed numbers.

disagreements.first_pass: Still the main prospective study of set, intentions and setting in self-directed psychedelic use found for this page. Its central acute finding, a better state of mind the day before going with fewer challenging experiences, agrees in direction with laboratory analyses that measured mood before dosing (Studerus 2012 for psilocybin, as described here; Studerus 2021 for MDMA; Vizeli 2024 for LSD), which is why the status is partial: those are conceptual replications in controlled settings with other instruments. No study has repeated the naturalistic prospective design with the same measures, and the well-being findings have no comparison group.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 269, missed: Discussion › Strengths, 1st paragraph: the authors describe the design as never before implemented in psychedelic research (as of 2018); the claims' 'the one prospective study' framing rests on this plus the editors' own knowledge of the literature, which the card could note under replication.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted: found as stated in the saved PMC copy. Sentence added; the claims now limit the phrase to the sources read (patch 280).
